_note: Name-facts for Italy (FT-36, docs/PLAN_V0.8.md). One file per country,
hand-authored, the only file here a person edits. Keyed by target id,
which is stable across every map that contains the place - Italy's
regions and its provinces share this file.
Each entry is a LIST, and the card shows a different one each time you
meet the place. The first is always about the NAME - where the word
comes from, who it is named after, what it meant - because the name is
the thing being learned and an etymology is the hook that holds it.
Later ones may be about the place instead.
Rules that keep these honest and useful:
- One sentence. The card has room for one line beneath the derived one.
- No fact the derived line already gives (position, coast, biggest city,
highest point, neighbours). Repeating it wastes the only spare line.
- Where an etymology is disputed, say so rather than picking a side.
- English only for now; the derived line above is already trilingual.
trentino-alto-adige: Two places in one name: Trento the city, and the upper valley of the Adige, the river that runs the length of it.
The only Italian region where most people in half of it speak German — the Alto Adige was Austrian until 1919.
friuli-venezia-giulia: Friuli is worn-down Latin Forum Iulii, "Julius's forum" — Julius Caesar's market town, now Cividale.
Venezia Giulia was coined in 1863 for the lands east of Venice, using Julius's name a second time in the same region.
veneto: Named for the Veneti, who were living here before Rome was — the same root as Venice itself.
The mainland that Venice ruled for four centuries; the city is the small part, the Veneto is the rest.
valle-d-aosta: The valley of Aosta, and Aosta is worn-down Augusta Praetoria — the town the Emperor Augustus founded in 25 BC.
Italy's smallest region, and the only one that is a single valley: one river, one road, walls of rock either side.
lombardia: Named for the Longobards, the "long-beards", a Germanic people who took northern Italy in 568 and ruled it for two centuries.
In the Middle Ages its bankers were so well known that a Lombard was a moneylender — London's Lombard Street is named after them.
piemonte: Literally "at the foot of the mountains" — ai piedi dei monti, the Alps that wrap it on three sides.
The kingdom that annexed the rest of Italy rather than joining it: Turin was the first capital of the unified country, in 1861.
emilia-romagna: Two halves, both named by Rome: the Via Aemilia, a road built in 187 BC and still the straight line through the region, and Romagna, the part that stayed Roman under Byzantium after the Longobards took the north.
The road is why almost every city here sits in a row: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, Rimini.
liguria: Named for the Ligures, who were here before the Romans and before the Celts — nobody is sure what language they spoke.
The Ligurian Sea is named after the region, not the other way round.
toscana: From the Tusci, the Roman name for the Etruscans, whose country this was before Rome had one.
Its dialect became the Italian language, because Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio all wrote in it.
marche: Plural because there were several: a march was a frontier province of the Holy Roman Empire, and this coast held more than one of them.
The same word as the English "marches" on the Welsh border, and as Denmark — the march of the Danes.
umbria: Named for the Umbri, an Italic people the Romans found here; the name is older than Latin.
The only region on the mainland with no coast and no foreign border — it touches nothing but other Italian regions.
abruzzo: From Aprutium, the medieval name of Teramo, which itself may come from the Praetutii who lived there.
A third of it is national park — the highest and wildest stretch of the Apennines, and the last place in Italy with wild bears.
lazio: Latium, the land of the Latins — the people whose village on the Tiber became Rome, and whose language became Latin.
Rome ruled an empire from here for a thousand years and the region is still named after the tribe, not the city.
molise: Named after a family, not a people: the Norman de Molisio counts held it in the twelfth century.
Italy's youngest region, split from Abruzzo in 1963, and its second smallest.
puglia: From Apulia, the Roman name for the land of the Apuli — and the heel of the boot.
Its trulli, the cone-roofed stone huts around Alberobello, were built dry-stone so they could be pulled down quickly when the tax inspector came.
campania: From Latin campus, "open country" — the Romans named it for its plain, the most fertile in Italy, and called it campania felix, the happy countryside.
The plain is fertile because Vesuvius keeps covering it in ash; the same volcano buried Pompeii in 79 AD.
basilicata: From Greek basilikos, "the emperor's man" — the Byzantine governor who ran it from Constantinople.
Also called Lucania, after the Lucani who were here first; Italy has changed the region's official name back and forth twice.
sardegna: Named for the Sardi, and they for Sardus, a legendary founder the Romans said came from Libya.
Its nuraghi — seven thousand dry-stone towers, some older than Rome — exist nowhere else on earth.
calabria: The name first belonged to the heel, not the toe: Roman Calabria was the Salento, and the name slid across the gulf in the Byzantine centuries.
Greek was still spoken in its southern villages into modern times, a survival from the colonies of Magna Graecia.
sicilia: Named for the Sicels, one of three peoples on the island when the Greeks arrived — the Sicani and the Elymians were the others.
Ruled in turn by Greeks, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Spaniards, and the food and the buildings still show every one of them.
